claim: Asthma is a dynamic disease in which lung mechanical and inflammatory processes interact in a complex manner, often resulting in exaggerated physiological, in particular, inflammatory responses to exogenous triggers.
source: Asthma is a dynamic disease, in which lung mechanical and inflammatory processes interact in a complex manner, often resulting in exaggerated physiological, in particular, inflammatory responses to exogenous triggers.
evidence: This is a general characterization of asthma presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Loss of adaptive capacity in asthma may be explained by respiratory disease-related systems instability and loss of adaptability to changing environmental conditions, manifested in highly fluctuating biomarkers and symptoms.
source: We hypothesize that this may be explained by respiratory disease-related systems instability and loss of adaptability to changing environmental conditions, manifested in highly fluctuating biomarkers and symptoms.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study, representing speculative reasoning about the mechanism underlying asthma.

claim: Loss of adaptive capacity was estimated by comparing similarities between pre- and post-challenge time series of inflammatory and clinical biomarkers.
source: Loss of AC was estimated by comparing similarities between pre- and post-challenge time series.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Unlike healthy participants, the asthmatic's post-viral-challenge state resembled more other rhinovirus-infected asthmatics than their own pre-viral-challenge state (hypergeometric-test: p=0.029).
source: Unlike healthy participants, the asthmatic's post-viral-challenge state resembled more other rhinovirus-infected asthmatics than their own pre-viral-challenge state (hypergeometric-test: p=0.029).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis (hypergeometric test with p-value) of experimental data.

claim: Loss of adaptive capacity in asthmatics reveals that biological processes underlying inflammatory and physiological responses are unstable, contributing to loss of control.
source: This reveals loss of AC and supports the concept that in asthma, biological processes underlying inflammatory and physiological responses are unstable, contributing to loss of control.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, drawing inferences from the experimental results.

claim: Physiologic systems have the ability to maintain a highly organized internal environment that is fluctuating within certain limits, despite being constantly exposed to a variable external environment.
source: The quantitative study of physiologic systems, such as the respiratory system, has revealed their ability to maintain a highly organized internal environment that is fluctuating within certain limits, despite being constantly exposed to a variable external environment (Que et al., 2001; Tirone and Brunicardi, 2001; Palmer and Clegg, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The term homeokinesis has been coined to describe the ability of physiologic systems to maintain fluctuating internal environments, substituting the concept of homeostasis.
source: The term homeokinesis has been coined to describe this ability, substituting the concept of homeostasis (Goldstein and Kopin, 2017) to emphasize that fluctuations in the internal environment are normal (Macklem, 2008; Macklem and Seely, 2010; Yates, 1982; Eke et al., 2002; Glass, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations defining and explaining the concept of homeokinesis.

claim: Homeokinesis is at the core of the observed adaptability, that is, adaptive capacity, of physiologic systems in response to changing environmental conditions.
source: Homeokinesis is at the core of the observed adaptability, that is, adaptive capacity, of physiologic systems in response to changing environmental conditions (Goldberger et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation linking homeokinesis to adaptive capacity.

claim: Homeokinesis is part of the remarkable complexity characteristic of physiologic systems, which is believed to originate from non-linear interactions and feedback-loops between their constitutive parts.
source: It is part of the remarkable complexity characteristic of such systems, which is believed to originate from non-linear interactions and feedback-loops between their constitutive parts (Goldberger et al., 2002; Garfinkel, 1983; Goldberger, 1996; Que, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations explaining the mechanistic basis of homeokinesis.

claim: Both excessive and too little variation in physiologic time series are indicative of pathological modifications and aging.
source: One of the most counterintuitive findings has been that both excessive and too little variation are indicative of pathological modifications and aging (Que et al., 2001; Goldberger et al., 2002 and references therein).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research findings.

claim: A chronic disease, such as asthma, may be understood as changes in the system that render it either too rigid or overly unstable.
source: Within this paradigm, a chronic disease, such as asthma, may be understood as changes in the system that render it either too rigid or overly unstable (Frey et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation providing a theoretical framework for understanding chronic disease.

claim: Disease or aging related changes of the system are accompanied by a loss of adaptive capacity.
source: Consequently, such disease or aging related changes of the system are accompanied by a loss of adaptive capacity (Goldberger et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation linking disease/aging to loss of adaptive capacity.

claim: Whether loss of adaptive capacity can be detected in asthmatics using longitudinal measurements of asthma-related biomarkers has never been investigated.
source: However, whether this can be detected in asthmatics using longitudinal measurements, that is time series, of asthma-related biomarkers has never been investigated.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature, establishing the novelty of the current study.

claim: Rhinovirus infections in asthmatics have been found to be among the most prominent external triggers of acute worsening of asthma symptoms, asthma exacerbations, and of loss of control.
source: This choice was driven by the fact that rhinovirus (RV) infections in asthmatics have been found to be among the most prominent external triggers of acute worsening of asthma symptoms, asthma exacerbations, and of loss of control (Johnston et al., 1995; Nicholson et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on rhinovirus and asthma.

claim: The capacity of rats to adapt to environmental heat stresses has been directly linked to the ability of the animal's liver cells to rapidly express the heat shock protein HSP70 in high quantities.
source: For instance, researchers have directly linked the capacity of rats to adapt to environmental heat stresses to the ability of the animal's liver cells to rapidly express the heat shock protein HSP70 in high quantities (Hall et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study on adaptive capacity in rats.

claim: Adaptive capacity has been defined as 'the capacity of a physiological system to bring itself autonomously back to the normal homeostatic range after a challenge'.
source: Other scientists have suggested 'the capacity of a physiological system to bring itself autonomously back to the normal homeostatic range after a challenge' as a more workable definition of adaptive capacity (Orešic and Vidal-Puig, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation providing a definition of adaptive capacity.

claim: In geriatric medicine, the definition of adaptive capacity as the ability to return to normal homeostatic range has been widely used, and the term homeostenosis was introduced to describe aging related loss of adaptive capacity.
source: Indeed, in geriatric medicine this definition has been widely used, and the term homeostenosis was introduced to describe aging related loss of adaptive capacity (Taffett, 2003; Fossion et al., 2018; Yashin et al., 2007; Fried et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to geriatric medicine literature.

claim: Adaptive capacity is defined as the ability of a physiological system to autonomously return to the normal homeokinetic range after an external challenge.
source: Based on these ideas, we define adaptive capacity as the ability of a physiological system to autonomously return to the normal homeokinetic range after an external challenge.
evidence: This is the operational definition adopted by the authors for their study.

claim: For a given biomarker, the post-viral-challenge time series of a study participant with an unimpaired adaptive capacity would resemble the same subject's pre-viral-challenge time series.
source: We hypothesized that, for a given biomarker, the post-viral-challenge time series of a study participant with an unimpaired adaptive capacity would resemble the same subject's pre-viral-challenge time series.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, representing speculative reasoning.

claim: The post-viral-challenge time series of a study participant with an impaired adaptive capacity would be relatively distinct from the same subject's pre-viral-challenge time series.
source: Conversely, the post-viral-challenge time series of a study participant with an impaired adaptive capacity would be relatively distinct from the same subject's pre-viral-challenge time series.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, representing speculative reasoning.

claim: Hierarchical clustering was used to group time series according to their relative similarity in an unassuming, data-driven manner.
source: In order to test this hypothesis, hierarchical clustering was used to group time series according to their relative similarity in an unassuming, data-driven manner.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The study found experimental evidence for the loss of adaptive capacity of the human respiratory system due to asthma.
source: With this approach we found experimental evidence for the loss of adaptive capacity of the human respiratory system due to asthma.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: In all cohort participants (12 healthy and 12 asthmatic volunteers), biomarkers were measured during two months before, and during one month immediately after deliberate experimental inoculation with rhinovirus.
source: In all cohort participants (12 healthy and 12 asthmatic volunteers), the biomarkers/parameters listed in Table 1 below were measured during two months before, and during one month immediately after deliberate experimental inoculation with rhinovirus, resulting in pre- and post-viral-challenge time series of each biomarker/parameter.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: Lung function (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC, PEF) was measured 2x daily before and after rhinovirus challenge.
source: Lung function (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC, PEF) 2x daily 2x daily
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 describing the sampling frequencies.

claim: Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO) was measured 3x weekly before and after rhinovirus challenge.
source: Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO) 3x weekly 3x weekly
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 describing the sampling frequencies.

claim: Eosinophil and neutrophil cell density in nasal lavage fluid was measured 1x weekly before rhinovirus challenge and 3x weekly after rhinovirus challenge.
source: Eosinophil and neutrophil cell density in nasal lavage fluid 1x weekly 3x weekly
evidence: This is stated in Table 1 describing the sampling frequencies.

claim: The Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) was used to quantitatively establish the degree of similarity or 'proximity' between two time series of a given biomarker.
source: In order to quantitatively establish the degree of similarity or 'proximity' between two time series of a given biomarker, we used the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD), which regards each of the time series as a univariate empirical distribution of the biomarker at hand (see Materials and methods and Appendix for more details).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Three clusters were found in the hierarchical clustering of FeNO time series.
source: In brief, we found three clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: Cluster 1 in the FeNO analysis consists of four time series stemming from two asthmatics.
source: Cluster 1 consists of four time series stemming from two asthmatics.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: The two asthmatic participants in Cluster 1 of the FeNO analysis are prominently different from the rest and might be regarded as outliers.
source: As can be read off of the dendrogram in Figure 1 below, and of the distance matrix depicted in Panel C of Figure 2 (see Materials and methods section below), these two participants are prominently different from the rest (regarding their FeNO time series), and might be regarded as outliers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the dendrogram and distance matrix shown in the figures.

claim: Cluster 2 in the FeNO analysis contains more healthy participants than expected by chance.
source: Cluster 2 contains more healthy participants than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Cluster 2 in the FeNO analysis is enriched in healthy participants.
source: In other words, Cluster 2 is enriched in healthy participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Cluster 2 in the FeNO analysis is depleted of asthmatic participants.
source: Conversely, due to the balanced design of the cohort (equal numbers of healthy and of asthmatic participants), Cluster 2 is also depleted of asthmatic participants, that is it contains fewer asthmatic participants than expected by chance.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: Cluster 3 in the FeNO analysis is enriched in asthmatic participants.
source: And finally, Cluster 3, which is enriched in asthmatic participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: All but one of the time series from healthy participants are grouped together in Cluster 2 of the FeNO analysis.
source: While all, but one, of the time series from healthy participants are grouped together in Cluster 2, the vast majority of time series from asthmatic participants are split into two different Clusters, namely Clusters 1 and 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: The vast majority of time series from asthmatic participants in the FeNO analysis are split into two different Clusters, namely Clusters 1 and 3.
source: While all, but one, of the time series from healthy participants are grouped together in Cluster 2, the vast majority of time series from asthmatic participants are split into two different Clusters, namely Clusters 1 and 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, as shown in Figure 1 and Table 2.

claim: The split of asthmatic time series into different clusters in the FeNO analysis suggests a higher heterogeneity among the asthmatics.
source: This suggest a higher heterogeneity among the asthmatics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering pattern observed in the data.

claim: In Cluster 2 of the FeNO analysis, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is statistically significant (p-value=0.007).
source: In Cluster 2, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is statistically significant (p-value=0.007, see Table 2 below).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: In Cluster 3 of the FeNO analysis, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is not statistically significant.
source: This is not the case for Cluster 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 2.

claim: On average, the cophenetic distances between the infected cluster members and their uninfected counterparts are statistically significantly lower in Cluster 2 when compared to Cluster 3 in the FeNO analysis (p-value=0.033, one-tailed Mann-Whitney-U-test).
source: The difference in this regard between Cluster 2 (mainly healthy participants) and Cluster 3 (mainly asthmatic participants) is further underpinned by the fact that, on average, the cophenetic distances (see Materials and methods section for the definition of cophenetic distance) between the infected cluster members and their uninfected counterparts are statistically significantly lower in Cluster 2 when compared to Cluster 3 (p-value=0.033, one-tailed Mann-Whitney-U-test, see Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of cophenetic distances.

claim: Cluster 2 in the FeNO analysis contains 1 fully represented asthmatic participant.
source: Fully represented asthmatic participants 1
evidence: This is stated in Table 2 for Cluster 2.

claim: Cluster 3 in the FeNO analysis contains 0 fully represented healthy participants.
source: Fully represented healthy participants 0
evidence: This is stated in Table 2 for Cluster 3.

claim: Within Cluster 3 of the FeNO analysis, the union of subclusters 3.1 and 3.2 is enriched in pre-challenge time series (p-value=0.029).
source: Indeed, the union of subclusters 3.1 and 3.2 is enriched in pre-challenge time series (p-value=0.029, see Table 3 below), whereas subcluster 3.3 is enriched in post-challenge time series (p-value=0.029, see Table 3 below).
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis of subclusters, as shown in Table 3.

claim: Within Cluster 3 of the FeNO analysis, subcluster 3.3 is enriched in post-challenge time series (p-value=0.029).
source: Indeed, the union of subclusters 3.1 and 3.2 is enriched in pre-challenge time series (p-value=0.029, see Table 3 below), whereas subcluster 3.3 is enriched in post-challenge time series (p-value=0.029, see Table 3 below).
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis of subclusters, as shown in Table 3.

claim: Such a separation of pre- and post-challenge time series cannot be observed within Cluster 2 of the FeNO analysis.
source: Such a separation cannot be observed within Cluster 2.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis of subclusters, as shown in Table 3.

claim: Three clusters were identified in the hierarchical clustering of percentage of eosinophils in nasal lavage fluid time series.
source: In brief, three clusters were identified.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 1 and Table 4.

claim: Cluster 1 in the eosinophil analysis consists of four time series stemming from three asthmatics.
source: Cluster 1 consists of four time series stemming from three asthmatics.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 1 and Table 4.

claim: The time series in Cluster 1 of the eosinophil analysis are prominently different from all the other time series, and might be regarded as outliers.
source: As can be read off of the dendrogram depicted in Appendix 1—figure 1, these time series are prominently different from all the other time series, and might be regarded as outliers.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the dendrogram shown in the figure.

claim: Cluster 2 in the eosinophil analysis is enriched in healthy participants.
source: Cluster 2 is enriched in healthy participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 4.

claim: Cluster 3 in the eosinophil analysis is enriched in asthmatic participants.
source: And finally, Cluster 3, which is enriched in asthmatic participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis, as shown in Table 4.

claim: In the eosinophil analysis, while the vast majority of the time series from healthy participants are grouped together in Cluster 2, most of the time series from asthmatic participants are split into two different Clusters, namely Clusters 1 and 3.
source: As seen in the analysis of FeNO, while the vast majority of the time series from healthy participants are grouped together in Cluster 2, most of the time series from asthmatic participants are split into two different Clusters, namely Clusters 1 and 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 1 and Table 4.

claim: The split of asthmatic time series into different clusters in the eosinophil analysis suggests a higher heterogeneity among the asthmatics.
source: This suggest a higher heterogeneity among the asthmatics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the clustering pattern observed in the data.

claim: Cluster 1 in the eosinophil analysis and Cluster 1 in the FeNO analysis only have one asthmatic patient in common.
source: However, Cluster 1 in the eosinophil analysis and Cluster 1 in the FeNO analysis only have one asthmatic patient in common.
evidence: This is a comparison of the clustering results across different biomarkers.

claim: In Cluster 2 of the eosinophil analysis, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is statistically significant (p-value=0.001).
source: Again, in Cluster 2, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is statistically significant (p-value=0.001, see Table 4 below).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 4.

claim: In Clusters 1 and 3 of the eosinophil analysis, the tendency for infected participants to be clustered together with their corresponding uninfected counterpart is not statistically significant.
source: This is not the case for Clusters 1 and 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis, as shown in Table 4.

claim: On average, the cophenetic distances between the infected cluster members and their uninfected counterparts are statistically significantly lower in Cluster 2 when compared to Cluster 3 in the eosinophil analysis (p-value=8.96e-05, one-tailed Mann-Whitney-U-test).
source: The difference in this regard between Cluster 2 (mainly healthy participants) and Cluster 3 (mainly asthmatic participants) is further substantiated by the fact that, on average, the cophenetic distances between the infected cluster members and their uninfected counterparts are statistically significantly lower in Cluster 2 when compared to Cluster 3 (p-value=8.96e-05, one-tailed Mann-Whitney-U-test, see Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of cophenetic distances.

claim: Cluster 2 in the eosinophil analysis contains 0 partially represented healthy participants.
source: Partially represented healthy participants 0
evidence: This is stated in Table 4 for Cluster 2.

source: Fully represented asthmatic participants 2
evidence: This is stated in Table 4 for Cluster 2.

source: Partially represented asthmatic participants 0

source: Partially represented asthmatic participants 2
evidence: This is stated in Table 4 for Cluster 3.

claim: For every participant, the autocorrelation coefficient of the lung function parameters time series and of the FeNO time series was calculated using a physiologically meaningful time lag.
source: For every participant, the autocorrelation coefficient of the lung function parameters time series and of the FeNO time series was calculated using a for each parameter type physiologically meaningful time lag.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: A one-day lag was used for lung function parameters in the autocorrelation analysis.
source: More specifically, a one-day lag was used for lung function parameters, and a two-days lag for FeNO.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: A two-days lag was used for FeNO in the autocorrelation analysis.
source: More specifically, a one-day lag was used for lung function parameters, and a two-days lag for FeNO.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: Due to the low sampling frequency used before the viral challenge, the time series of eosinophil and neutrophil cell density in nasal lavage fluid were not included in the autocorrelation analysis.
source: Due to the low sampling frequency used before the viral challenge, the time series of eosinophil and neutrophil cell density in nasal lavage fluid were not included in the autocorrelation analysis.
evidence: This explains a methodological limitation.

claim: In terms of autocorrelation, the lung function parameters PEF (% predicted), FVC, and FEV1/FVC discriminate significantly between the pre- and post-infection status in both healthy and asthmatic participants.
source: Briefly, in terms of autocorrelation, the lung function parameters PEF (% predicted), FVC, and FEV1/FVC discriminate significantly between the pre- and post-infection status in both healthy and asthmatic participants.
evidence: This is a finding from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: For PEF (% predicted), FVC, and FEV1/FVC, there is a moderate positive autocorrelation before the challenge, which then disappears after the challenge.
source: Indeed, for these three parameters, there is a moderate positive autocorrelation before the challenge, which then disappears after the challenge.
evidence: This is a finding from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: In terms of autocorrelation, only FeNO discriminates significantly between healthy and asthmatic participants, and it does so only after the challenge.
source: Furthermore, in terms of autocorrelation, only FeNO discriminates significantly between healthy and asthmatic participants, and it does so only after the challenge.
evidence: This is a finding from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: Only asthmatics exhibit a moderate autocorrelation of their FeNO time series after the challenge.
source: More specifically, only asthmatics exhibit a moderate autocorrelation of their FeNO time series after the challenge.
evidence: This is a finding from the autocorrelation analysis.

claim: After multiple pairwise-comparison correction, only the parameters FVC and FEV1/FVC discriminate significantly between the pre- and post-infection status in both healthy and asthmatic participants.
source: However, after a multiple pairwise-comparison correction aimed at controlling the false discovery rate, only the parameters FVC and FEV1/FVC discriminate significantly between the pre- and post-infection status in both healthy and asthmatic participants, while the other findings lose their statistical significance.
evidence: This is a finding from the autocorrelation analysis after correction for multiple testing.

claim: 11 out of 12 healthy participants were effectively infected with the RV16 after inoculation according to blood antibody tests and RV PCR.
source: Indeed, the results of blood antibody tests (RV16 seroconversion) along with RV Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) conducted on nasal lavage fluid taken from every participant after the inoculation indicated that 11 out of 12 healthy participants and 12 out of 12 asthmatics were effectively infected with the RV16 after inoculation (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from laboratory tests confirming the efficacy of the viral challenge.

claim: 12 out of 12 asthmatics were effectively infected with the RV16 after inoculation according to blood antibody tests and RV PCR.
source: Indeed, the results of blood antibody tests (RV16 seroconversion) along with RV Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) conducted on nasal lavage fluid taken from every participant after the inoculation indicated that 11 out of 12 healthy participants and 12 out of 12 asthmatics were effectively infected with the RV16 after inoculation (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from laboratory tests confirming the efficacy of the viral challenge.

claim: One healthy participant did not become infected according to laboratory tests, but developed cold symptoms within a few days after the virus inoculation, suggesting that the laboratory tests failed to detect the ongoing infection.
source: According to the above mentioned laboratory tests, one healthy participant did not become infected. However, this participant did develop cold symptoms within a few days after the virus inoculation, suggesting that the laboratory tests failed to detect the ongoing infection although the participant was positively infected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of clinical and laboratory findings.

claim: The healthy participant who did not show infection by laboratory tests was included in the analyses.
source: Consequently, this participant was included in the analyses.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision based on clinical judgment.

claim: Two different criteria for 'responders' were implemented to assess within-subject changes upon infection.
source: To this end, two criteria for 'responders' were implemented.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the responder analysis.

claim: The first criterion for responders aimed at detecting distributional changes in a given biomarker induced by the viral challenge using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
source: The first criterion, which regards time series as univariate empirical distributions of the biomarker at hand, aimed at detecting distributional changes in a given biomarker induced by the viral challenge: Here, each participant's pre- and post-challenge time series of each biomarker were compared using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the responder analysis.

claim: The second criterion for responders aimed at detecting short-term and transient relative changes induced by the viral challenge in the context of the relative changes observed prior to the challenge.
source: The second criterion aimed at detecting short-term and transient relative changes induced by the viral challenge in the context of the relative changes observed prior to the challenge.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the responder analysis.

claim: The study provided experimental evidence for the loss of adaptive capacity in the human respiratory system due to asthma.
source: In this proof of concept study, we provided experimental evidence for the loss of adaptive capacity in the human respiratory system due to asthma.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: FeNO and eosinophil time series were similar prior to and following the challenge in healthy subjects, suggesting stable homeokinetic behavior.
source: Using a data-driven clustering approach, we have shown that, in particular, FeNO and eosinophil time series were similar prior to and following the challenge in healthy subjects, suggesting stable homeokinetic behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: In asthmatics, the similarity between pre- and post-challenge FeNO and eosinophil time series was predominantly reduced, suggesting a marked impact of the asthmatic condition on dynamic properties of the respiratory system.
source: In asthmatics, however, this similarity was predominantly reduced, suggesting a marked impact of the asthmatic condition on dynamic properties of the respiratory system, consistent with more unstable behavior and loss of adaptive capacity following the perturbation with viral infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: The loss of self-similarity in asthmatics is not merely the result of a larger response to the virus infection.
source: This loss of self-similarity is not merely the result of a larger response to the virus infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Changes in the overall biomarker fluctuation dynamics elicited by the viral challenge render asthmatics more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their uninfected counterparts.
source: Rather, we detected changes in the overall biomarker fluctuation dynamics elicited by the viral challenge that render asthmatics more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their uninfected counterparts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: Evidence was found for the tendency of infected asthmatic participants to be more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their own uninfected counterparts when similarity is measured in terms of the biomarker dynamics of FeNO.
source: Summarizing, we have found evidence for the tendency of infected asthmatic participants to be more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their own uninfected counterparts when similarity is measured in terms of the biomarker dynamics of FeNO, of the percentage of eosinophils in nasal lavage fluid, and of cell density in nasal lavage fluid.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Evidence was found for the tendency of infected asthmatic participants to be more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their own uninfected counterparts when similarity is measured in terms of the biomarker dynamics of the percentage of eosinophils in nasal lavage fluid.
source: Summarizing, we have found evidence for the tendency of infected asthmatic participants to be more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their own uninfected counterparts when similarity is measured in terms of the biomarker dynamics of FeNO, of the percentage of eosinophils in nasal lavage fluid, and of cell density in nasal lavage fluid.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Evidence was found for the tendency of infected asthmatic participants to be more similar to other infected asthmatic participants than to their own uninfected counterparts when similarity is measured in terms of the biomarker dynamics of cell density in nasal lavage fluid.

claim: Time series of lung function over days display a weak intrinsic autocorrelation over long- and short-time scales in asthmatic and healthy subjects.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lung function is correlated with lung function values of previous days.

claim: Correlation properties of lung function are related to severity of asthma and disease control.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Following the viral challenge, the lung mechanical system properties are less deterministic consistent with a lower stability of the respiratory system.

claim: Epidemiological observations have questioned the simple causal relationship between mechanisms in asthma (e.g. viral trigger → inflammation → bronchial hyperreactivity→ airway obstruction→ respiratory symptoms).

claim: After RV challenge lung function in asthmatic subjects did change, but did not decline dramatically in comparison to the changes observed in healthy controls.

claim: Data from a previous study show that a low dose of RV16 is sufficient to induce mild cold-symptoms.
source: Data from our previous study show that a low dose is sufficient to induce mild cold-symptoms (Mallia et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A low-dose inoculum of RV16 previously resulted in a slight decrease of FEV1 (loss of asthma control) in asthmatic patients between day 4 and 6 after RV16 exposure, whereas no decrease has been observed in healthy controls.
source: Furthermore, this low-dose inoculum previously resulted in a slight decrease of FEV1 (loss of asthma control) in asthmatic patients between day 4 and 6 after RV16 exposure, whereas no decrease has been observed in healthy controls (Grünberg et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Statistical tests resulting in a p-value less or equal to 0.05 were regarded as significant.
source: Statistical tests resulting in a p-value less or equal to 0.05 were regarded as significant.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: For each participant, their time series of a given biomarker prior to and after the viral challenge were compared using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
source: For each participant, their time series of a given biomarker prior to and after the viral challenge were compared. This comparison was based on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, whereby the time series were treated as empirical distributions, thus disregarding the chronological order of the measurements.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: Differences in the variance between the pre- and post-challenge distributions were assessed using Levene's test.
source: Differences in the variance between the pre- and post-challenge distributions were assessed using Levene's test (Levene, 1961).
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple comparison correction was performed where required, using the false discovery rate (FDR) method of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), setting the expected proportion of falsely rejected null hypotheses to 0.05.
source: Multiple comparison correction was performed where required, using the false discovery rate (FDR) method of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), setting the expected proportion of falsely rejected null hypotheses to 0.05.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The time series of a given biomarker, prior to and after the viral challenge, were regarded as empirical distributions and compared to each other using the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD).
source: The time series of a given biomarker, prior to and after the viral challenge, were regarded as empirical distributions and compared to each other using the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) (Rubner et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The resulting pair-wise distances between distributions were then used for hierarchical clustering of pre- and post-challenge distributions.
source: The resulting pair-wise distances between distributions were then used for hierarchical clustering of pre- and post-challenge distributions.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The clustering approach makes use of the entire time series (distributions) of values measured before and after the challenge, respectively, and does not amalgamate the information into a single magnitude.
source: Our clustering approach makes use of the entire time series (distributions) of values measured before and after the challenge, respectively, and does not amalgamate the information into a single magnitude (e.g., the mean value).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The clustering method unveils subtle differences and similarities between the participants' measurements that are less likely to be captured by conventional methods based on averages.
source: This method unveils subtle differences and similarities between the participants' measurements that are less likely to be captured by conventional methods based on averages.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the methodological approach.

claim: For each participant individually, and for each biomarker, throughout the entire period of observation, the biomarker's relative change in value taking place within time intervals of 10 days was calculated.
source: For each participant individually, and for each biomarker, throughout the entire period of observation, the biomarker's relative change in value taking place within time intervals of 10 days was calculated.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The choice of 10 day time interval length was made based on published literature whereby 5 days post exposure to respiratory viruses was shown to be critical.
source: This choice of time interval length was made based on published literature whereby 5 days post exposure to respiratory viruses was shown to be critical. Hence a 10 day window for comparison would include 5 days before challenge to contrast with 5 days after challenge (Denlinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the rationale for the methodological choice, supported by a citation.

claim: In order to evaluate the discriminatory power of a given biomarker, the clusters found in the clustering dendrogram were tested for enrichment in or depletion of healthy or asthmatic participants, and/or for enrichment in or depletion of pre- or post-challenge distributions.
source: In order to evaluate the discriminatory power of a given biomarker, the clusters found in the clustering dendrogram were tested for enrichment in or depletion of healthy or asthmatic participants, and/or for enrichment in or depletion of pre- or post-challenge distributions.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Statistically significant enrichment or depletion were established using the hypergeometric test.
source: Statistically significant enrichment or depletion were established using the hypergeometric test (Rubner et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The relative location of leaves in the clustering dendrogram was quantitatively evaluated using the cophenetic distance.
source: The relative location of leaves in the clustering dendrogram was quantitatively evaluated using the cophenetic distance (Sokal and Rohlf, 1962).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: The cophenetic distance between two leaves of a dendrogram is defined as the height of the dendrogram at which the two largest branches that individually contain the two leaves merge into a single branch.
source: The cophenetic distance between two leaves of a dendrogram is defined as the height of the dendrogram at which the two largest branches that individually contain the two leaves merge into a single branch.
evidence: This is a definition of a technical term used in the analysis.

claim: If the disruption caused by the viral challenge is not strong enough, the pre- and post-challenge distributions of a given participant will tend to cluster together.
source: If the disruption caused by the viral challenge is not strong enough, the pre- and post-challenge distributions of a given participant will tend to cluster together.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: A cluster in which pre- and post-pairs are closely located in terms of the cophenetic distance within the dendrogram, represents a subgroup of participants for which the viral challenge caused a relatively weaker disruption.
source: Therefore, a cluster in which pre- and post-pairs are closely located in terms of the cophenetic distance within the dendrogram, represents a subgroup of participants for which the viral challenge caused a relatively weaker disruption, at least with respect to the biomarker under scrutiny.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the interpretation of the clustering results.

claim: Two dendrogram leaves are called neighbors if their mutual cophenetic distance is equal to the minimum of all cophenetic distances from one of the leaves to all the other leaves in the dendrogram.
source: Two dendrogram leaves are called neighbors if their mutual cophenetic distance is equal to the minimum of all cophenetic distances from one of the leaves to all the other leaves in the dendrogram.
evidence: This is a definition of a technical term used in the analysis.

claim: Under the null-hypothesis that the branching in the dendrogram is the result of a purely random process, the number of neighboring pre- and post-pairs to be expected just by chance within a given cluster can be estimated by simply permuting the labels of the leaves in the dendrogram and counting the number of neighboring pre- and post-pairs.
source: Under the null-hypothesis that the branching in the dendrogram is the result of a purely random process, the number of neighboring pre- and post-pairs to be expected just by chance within a given cluster can be estimated by simply permuting the labels of the leaves in the dendrogram and counting the number of neighboring pre- and post-pairs.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: The permutation test is used for calculating the empirical p-values displayed in Tables 2 and 4.
source: This permutation test is used for calculating the empirical p-values displayed in Tables 2 and 4 above.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used in the study.

claim: The autocorrelation of a given time series was calculated using the sample Pearson correlation coefficient of the original time series and the time series resulting after forward-shifting the original time series by the lag utilized.
source: The autocorrelation of a given time series was calculated using the sample Pearson correlation coefficient of the original time series and the time series resulting after forward-shifting the original time series by the lag utilized.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the autocorrelation analysis.
